background: In August 2026, the digital health company Sharecare was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign . The group subsequently published data it claimed was taken from Sharecare's systems, containing 318k unique email addresses. Most of the data consisted of B2B sales and marketing records with names, physical addresses, phone numbers, job titles and employers.
The data also included a small number of Brazilian health insurance plan members, including dates of birth, genders, marital statuses and CPF numbers (Brazilian taxpayer identification numbers).
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In August 2026, the digital health company Sharecare was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion campaign .
outcome: 318,185 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Employers, Genders, Government issued IDs, Job titles, Marital statuses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: Most of this data is B2B sales and marketing records, the same kind of business contact list that appears in several other ShinyHunters releases. Read only the headline and you would file it as a nuisance. The detail that changes that is in the last line of the record: a small number of Brazilian health plan members, with dates of birth, genders, marital statuses and CPF numbers.

A CPF is Brazil's taxpayer identification number, and it is used far more widely than its name suggests: opening bank accounts, signing up for phone contracts, buying online, and proving identity to almost any service. Paired with a name and date of birth it is enough to attempt credit and account fraud in that person's name.

A small number of records can carry more real harm than hundreds of thousands of work email addresses. That is a pattern worth recognising in breach reporting generally. The size of a set and its severity are different measurements. If you hold a Brazilian plan connected to Sharecare, monitoring your CPF for new credit activity matters more here than changing any password.

The B2B majority of the file has its own, more ordinary risk. For a digital health company, sales and marketing records are likely to describe the people who buy health services on behalf of others, such as benefits managers, HR leads and plan administrators.

Those are the people who receive genuine messages about enrolment periods and programme renewals, which makes them a natural audience for a fake renewal invoice or a fake "update your plan portal login" email. The record also shows how far a single incident can travel across borders.

A United States digital health company, a criminal group publishing worldwide, and a small group of Brazilian plan members whose CPF numbers ended up in the same release. Data protection law in Brazil (the LGPD) and in the United States treats those records very differently, but the people in them face the same practical question: whether anyone has used their details to open something new.
For the Brazilian members, checking for credit or accounts opened in your CPF is the step that answers it.

fields.name: Government issued IDs
fields.why: Passport and licence numbers are used to prove identity to banks and telecoms, and they are effectively permanent.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Dates of birth
fields.why: One of the three things call centres ask to verify identity, and it never changes.

fields.name: Employers
fields.why: Connects a personal account to a workplace, which is how attackers pivot from a person to a company.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: An exposed address may be used in phishing attempts. Treat unexpected messages with caution.

fields.name: Job titles
fields.why: Identifies who has access to what, which is how targets for business email compromise are picked.

fields.name: Marital statuses
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

fields.name: Genders
fields.why: Small on its own; useful to anyone assembling a fuller profile.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Consider a credit freeze. A government identifier cannot be changed, so limiting what can be opened in your name is the only real control.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Be alert to phishing. A message may use details from exposed or collected records to appear familiar; verify requests through the service directly.
